## Introduction

- March Madness is a $68$-team, single-elimination tournament across both the Men's and Women's divisions to determine the NCAA National Champions.

\vspace{0.2in}

- The Kaggle competition (March Machine Learning Mania) evaluates the accuracy of predictions using the Brier score (BS).

\vspace{0.2in}

\begin{equation}
BS = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^N(f_t - o_t)^2
\end{equation}
\begin{itemize}
\item Where $f_t$ is our prediction and $o_t$ is the outcome. 
\item $o_t$ is $1$ if the team wins, and $0$ is they lose. 
\end{itemize}

## Introduction

\begin{itemize}
\item A naive `coin flip' strategy (50\% probability for all games) yields a Brier Score of $0.25$, serving as our baseline.
\vspace{0.2in}
\begin{example}
If we predict that Duke has a win probability of $0.70$ against Houston.

If Duke \textcolor{red}{wins},
$$\text{Cost} = (\textcolor{red}{1}-0.70)^2 = (0.3)(0.3) = 0.09$$
If Duke \textcolor{red}{loses},
$$\text{Cost} = (\textcolor{red}{0}-0.70)^2 = (0.7)(0.7) = 0.49$$
\end{example}
\vspace{0.2in}
\item We will call the two teams we are predicting Team A and team B. 
\end{itemize}
## Models
\begin{itemize}
\item We looked at three different modeling techniques:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Two models gave us the probability outright (Logistic/XGBoost).
  \item One model predicted the final scores (Simulation).
  \end{itemize}
\vspace{0.2in}
\item We will be looking at the model that predicts final scores. We separate the men's and women's divisions.

\vspace{0.2in}
\item We are predicting the points that Team A will score against team B and vice versa. Then simulate $+50,000$ times. 
\item The ratio that Team A wins of the simulation is the predicted probability.
\end{itemize}

## Models
\begin{columns}
\column{0.5\textwidth}
\textbf{Men's Model}
\begin{itemize}
\item Offensive Rating ($OffRating_A$)
\item Defensive Rating ($DefRating_B$)
\item Team Tempo ($AdjTempo_A$)
\item Opponent Tempo ($AdjTempo_B$)
\item Net Rating Difference ($NetRating_A - NetRating_B$)
\item Elo Difference ($Elo_A - Elo_B$)
\end{itemize}

\column{0.5\textwidth}
\textbf{Women's Model}
\begin{itemize}
\item Offensive Rating ($OffRating_A$)
\item Defensive Rating ($DefRating_B$)
\item Team Tempo ($AdjTempo_A$)
\item Opponent Tempo ($AdjTempo_B$)
\item Elo Difference ($Elo_A - Elo_B$)
\end{itemize}
\end{columns}

## 2025 Results
\begin{itemize}
    \item Model Achieved a Brier Score of \textcolor{red}{$0.1305$} ($500$ spots away from bronze).
    \vspace{0.1in}
    \item Men's tournament Brier score was \textcolor{red}{$0.1448$}. Women's was \textcolor{red}{$0.1157$}.
    \vspace{0.1in}
    \item Winning scores for the past three years were:
\end{itemize}
\begin{table}
    \centering
    \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.5}
    \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
        \hline
        \textbf{2023} & \textbf{2024} & \textbf{2025} \\
        \hline
        0.1737 & 0.0531 & \textcolor{red}{$0.1041$} \\
        \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \caption{Winning Brier Scores}
\end{table}

## 2025 Results
\begin{itemize}
\item The 2025 Model was $79.9\%$ accurate in picking the winners and losers. 

\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.5\linewidth]{2025_lin_reg_monte_womens-8.pdf}

## 2026 Results
\begin{itemize}
\item Prior to the tournament, we made $32$ overrides to the models predictions. These were to give $100\%$ probability to obvious favorites. 
\vspace{0.2in}
\item Got $30$ overrides correct, missed $2$.
\vspace{0.2in}
\begin{table}
    \centering
    \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.5}
    \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
        \hline
        \textbf{Overrides} & \textbf{Original} & \textbf{Winner} \\
        \hline
        0.13237 & 0.12797 & \textcolor{red}{$0.10975$} \\
        \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \caption{2026 Brier Score Comparisons}
\end{table}
\vspace{0.2in}
\item These probabilities were $63.6\%, 64.2\%, 66.9\%$ correct. 
\end{itemize}

## 2026 Results
\begin{itemize}
\item The 2026 Model was $77.8\%$ accurate.
\end{itemize}
